item.title: In Its Race to Field AI, The Pentagon’s Testing Can’t Keep Up
item.description:
CNN reported, citing four sources familiar with the episode, that the U.S. military prepared to intercept a Chinese vessel after an AI-assisted intelligence report misidentified its cargo. According to CNN, the report incorrectly concluded that the ship was carrying components of a nuclear weapons program. Some of CNN’s sources said troops prepared to board the vessel and military aircraft were already airborne. Officials discovered the error before the planned operation. CNN could not establish which chatbot the analyst used and reported that the Pentagon and U.S. Special Operations Command Pacific did not respond to its requests for comment.

Military organizations use different tools and standards to check AI-generated information. As CNN reported, there is "no one set of standards for how the US verifies the information generated by these tools." The January 2026 AI Acceleration Strategy directs that the department enable “the latest models to be deployed within 30 days of public release". The model behind any application can change every month, but the definition of a correct answer should not. The fix, and the department's best path to AI safety, is to put guardrails in place by testing the systems built on these models the same way the department tests everything else it fields: against a written specification, by someone who does not work for the vendor, with evidence that outlasts any one model.

Scott Cohen is co-founder and CEO of Jaxon.AI, which sells AI verification and validation tools, including under Air Force and Space Force contracts. Jen Warren advises Jaxon.AI. The company could benefit financially if the Pentagon adopts the testing requirements recommended in this article.

A Model Is a Component

The department is dedicated to fielding AI quickly and widely. GenAI.mil launched in December 2025 with Google's Gemini; by September 2026 it had 1.7 million users. ChatGPT and Grok were added August 31, 2026. Users have built more than 100,000 custom agents since launch. On September 23, 2026, the deputy under secretary for research and engineering said the department will "proliferate frontier models" onto the secret and top secret networks next.

The directive on autonomy in weapon systems requires that "any further changes to the system will undergo appropriate V&V and T&E," that is, verification and validation, and test and evaluation. The department's own testers admit in a 2025 guidebook that "T&E of GenAI is still in its infancy as a discipline." The whole field shares the problem. Generative AI is particularly hard to test because a traditional test compares a system's output to a known right answer, and generative AI writes answers no one has seen before. There is no answer key to check them against.

The eight public announcements we reviewed, issued between December 2025 and September 23, 2026, did not disclose what performance tests GenAI.mil models underwent, what standards applied, or who signed off on fielding them. Every announcement cites Impact Level 5 accreditation instead, and the Chief Information Officer's July 2025 guide points out: "AI models do not need an ATO [authority to operate], but the actual system infrastructure layer does," and "adding models to an already approved system will typically not require a new system authorization." The same guide clarifies that it covers cybersecurity only and excludes "AI system performance expectations." The accreditation covers the hosting environment.

Military AI users number in the millions, yet the department cut its independent operational test organization's staff in half. The Government Accountability Office found in April that "well-defined, universal AI tests do not exist yet," and in June that this cut "increases the risk of weapon systems being delivered to the warfighters with undocumented shortfalls." In a January 12 speech, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth named test and evaluation and authority to operate among the barriers to be "treated as operational risks." Three senators called for an inspector general investigation into the intelligence report based on faulty AI answers.

The Models Will Keep Surprising Their Makers

Testing the system is better than testing the model because AI vendors cannot predict what their own models will do. OpenAI reported that models in an internal cybersecurity evaluation bypassed isolation controls and compromised parts of its research infrastructure and Hugging Face’s systems in July 2026. OpenAI described how agents used a shared message board to exchange exploits. The incident illustrates how a model can behave in ways its developers did not anticipate.

The frontier labs' safety remedies (red lines, better alignment, more monitoring by more models) are all model-level. The department’s strategy calls for the ability to deploy new models within thirty days of release. It should also spell out how those models will be tested independently in military applications. Anthropic proposed embedding outside evaluators, arguing that a second opinion "free of commercial incentives" beats any self-report. The department should apply independent verification to models used in the military, especially any that are used in or inform the killweb.

What a System Test Looks Like, and Who Runs It

The department has made AI available to millions of users. Its public GenAI.mil announcements give little detail about how it tests system performance. A weapon system has to pass an independent operational test before it is fielded. An analyst's finished intelligence product has to meet assurance standards in Intelligence Community Directive 203: document how good the sources are, and keep what is known apart from what is assumed. The department should apply a comparable retesting requirement when it swaps a model in an AI system.

AI systems should be tested the way any other system is: define what right looks like, run a test to verify it behaves as expected, and document the evidence for future reviews. The returned verdict should pass or fail against a documented test metric, while demonstrating the strength of evidence the verdict rests on. A pass on thin evidence should never be mistaken for a pass on all related questions, and a test with no evidence to rule on should say so rather than pass by default. This test survives a model swap because the specification lives outside the model. The specification says what a correct output looks like for this system.

Swap Gemini for ChatGPT for Grok and the specification does not change, so the same specification is run again against the new model, and the comparison shows whether the swap moved the system's behavior, and by how much. The objection that you cannot test a system whose core component changes every month gets it backward. The component is the thing you cannot certify, because it will be different next month. The specification is the thing that stays put, and running it again after every change is the only test that still means anything once the swap has happened.

A test for an intelligence system could check whether cited evidence actually supports a claim about a ship’s cargo. That would help test for the kind of error CNN described.

Some have argued that military units using AI should handle testing themselves, with a single authorized operator who logs prompts, keeps a small test set, tunes prompts until the model’s answers look right, and rolls back a model that is inaccurate or drifting. That is a poor force-wide answer for four reasons: (1) it makes one person in each unit a single point of failure, applied differently across the force, which complicates multi-theater operations; (2) the judgment behind those prompts leaves with every operator's change of station, and the prompts left behind were tuned for a model that’s constantly changing; (3) units lack the authority to roll back a model in a system shared across organizations; and (4) a prompt tuned for one AI model fails on the next, while the department runs several vendors' models concurrently.

Vendor benchmarks alone cannot establish whether an AI system meets a military mission’s requirements. For weapons, operational testing is independent of the program office by law, because a program office and its vendor have every incentive to report that performance meets the requirement. A system test for AI needs the same independence: a tester that owns the specification, runs it on every model change, and reports to the authorizing official. That tester can be the Director of Operational Test and Evaluation, a service operational test agency, a federally funded research and development center, a university-affiliated research center, a contracted third party, or a combination thereof. It has to answer to the government and must have no stake in the model under test. The tools for writing and running a specification are a secondary question. Several already exist, and the United Kingdom’s AI Security Institute has released one as open source.

Critics may argue that thirty days is too short to verify a model. That assumes every model swap triggers a scheduled test event, with testers, test windows, and a written report. A specification-based test needs none of that. When a model changes, so does every system that runs on it, such as a custom agent on GenAI.mil or an intelligence system built on the same model. No test workforce, let alone one just cut in half, could review thousands of systems every month. Running a specification-based test doesn't depend on that workforce’s daily capacity, because the specification is programmed once and reruns at machine speed. The systems with the new model undergo the programmed tests, the testing software scores the answers, and the results are delivered to accreditors. Systems that fail stay on the currently approved model while the vendor fixes the model release that failed. The test specification is updated on its own schedule, as the mission changes or test results reveal gaps, and never to fit a particular model.

Write It Down, Fund It, and Own It

Program offices that want AI safety run into the same challenges as most programs: no documented requirement and insufficient authorized and appropriated funding. First, the requirement: the acceleration strategy tells vendors to deliver the newest model, fast, and is silent on verifying outputs by a tester. It should also require that the system be tested against the command's written specification by a government or independent tester, with a record. It is imperative this testing happens before a model is fielded for any use that produces finished intelligence or feeds targeting, and after every model change. That language can go into the next GenAI.mil model release tomorrow, rather than wait for the standards Congress has ordered by June 2027. Second, the money: the department should identify funding for the testing it requires. The department already knows what a failure costs.

Currently, authorizing officials accredit system infrastructure, not the AI models within, nor the answers they produce. The department should make the AI's performance part of what is authorized, similar to how a weapon must meet accuracy thresholds. The definition of a correct answer, the test evidence, and the record should travel with the authorization package, and a model swap that fails against them should be reworked before it is fielded. This approach mirrors what the autonomy directive already requires for weapons. Extending it to the intelligence tools that inform what those weapons do is the same requirement, applied one step earlier.

Specifications, Checks, and a Record

We are not arguing the department should slow down AI implementation. All military users should have the power of AI. What the department should prevent is a wrong answer that tears a hole in the killweb.

The senators called for the inspectors general to investigate. Any investigation comes down to three questions: what were the specifications, who checked the systems met these specifications, and where is the record. Right now, the department can answer the first with a stack of directives and the other two with a shrug. Corrective action is straightforward and ready to implement immediately. The department can update the policy to require that AI models be tested for accuracy, specifying that contracts be updated to reflect this requirement, then apply funding to address this pressing operational need. Improving AI safety will directly drive operational outcomes and protect the department and its people from being misled by AI hallucinations.

item.title: The midterms were a referendum on Trump—and Biden—foreign policy
item.description:
There is no debate as to why Donald Trump and the Republican Party suffered a historic and humiliating defeat at the polls on Tuesday: it all comes down to the Iran war and the cost-of-living crisis it has brought about.

But lost in the conversation is that this was not just a rejection of the Iran war. It was also a repudiation of the broader foreign policy that repeatedly gets the U.S. into wars — or into supporting the wars and war crimes of U.S. partners. In many contests on Tuesday, the U.S.-Israel relationship was on the ballot too, and it was rejected by Republicans and Democrats alike in favor of recentering priorities back to national interests, including ending the flow of military aid to Israel.

Trump famously ran on a promise to end forever wars and not to start new ones. But he ended up listening to the Israeli Prime Minister and started a major war with Iran, even though a diplomatic deal was on the table that was objectively stronger than President Barack Obama’s deal. Trump could have declared victory, but instead he listened to the Israeli government and chose to declare war. Now he is paying for it by losing his majority in Congress.

But it’s not just this election. Since George W. Bush, the American public has voted for presidents — Obama, then Trump and Biden — who have promised less foreign adventurism and more military restraint. Now, with a rejection of the Gaza policy in 2024 and now Iran in 2026, wars are becoming a major, even crucial factor in their voting, according to exit polling.

President Joe Biden repeatedly touted the centrality of human rights in his foreign policy. "That's why, from day one of my administration, I've taken concrete steps to put human rights back at the center of our foreign policy," he said in a speech in October 2021. But when push came to shove, Biden deferred to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and ended up funding and enabling a genocide in Gaza.

A year later, voters punished the Democrats at the polls and paved the way for Trump’s return to the White House.

A YouGov–IMEU Policy Project poll in January 2025 found that, of the 2020 Biden voters who chose not to vote in 2024, a plurality stayed home because of the Democrats’ Gaza policy. Axios reported that the Democrats' own internal election autopsy reportedly concluded Gaza cost them the elections.

So when voters in Texas elect a candidate who proudly rejects money from the America Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) and says that “seeing what's happening in Gaza makes me sick to my stomach as a teacher, as a Christian, as a human being,” and when voters in Michigan cheer when their Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed accuses Israel of genocide and apartheid in his victory speech, it is not just a rejection of Trump’s war; it is also a rejection of the foreign policy of Joe Biden, Antony Blinken, and Jake Sullivan.

Both Trump and Biden, in various ways and to various degrees, pursued a hegemonic foreign policy that continued rather than broke with decades of militarism and deference to Israel. And both Trump and Biden’s voters have now rejected this policy paradigm, revalidating the basis for a transpartisan — or postpartisan — push for a new foreign-policy framework centered on responsible statecraft that seeks strength through peace and prosperity through coexistence.

Opportunities for collaboration between Republicans and Democrats responsive to these overwhelming sentiments of the American people will be plentiful in the next two years.

But the first test will be on December 11, when the current continuing resolution for federal government funding expires. Congress has an obligation now to insist on no new money for the Iran War if and when they pass another stopgap to avoid a shutdown.

item.title: ‘Very clear that China isn’t neutral’ in Ukraine war, says former Ukrainian Prime Minister Arseniy Yatsenyuk
item.description:
‘Very clear that China isn’t neutral’ in Ukraine war, says former Ukrainian Prime Minister Arseniy Yatsenyuk News release thilton.drupal 5 November 2026

Speaking at a public event at Chatham House, Yatsenyuk also suggested it was unrealistic that Ukraine could regain territory ‘right now’ and called for additional financial support.

Ukraine’s former prime minister Arseniy Yatsenyuk said that Chinese support for Russia was helping it to continue the Ukraine war as he discussed the war’s trajectory at Chatham House on Tuesday 3 November.  

Yatsenyuk said that while the Russian economy is in a ‘dire state’, Russia’s president Vladimir Putin still has ‘enough resources to prosecute the war.’ He said the reasons for this included higher oil prices due to the Iran war and Chinese support for Russia.

Yatsenyuk said:

‘I want to be very clear that China isn’t neutral. China actually supports this war, and China is an ally to Russia. Let’s call a spade a spade.  

I do understand that it’s around 1.5 billion of people, nukes, a huge global powerhouse. But the truth is that China is actually the closest strategic partner to the Russian Federation, and China provided the way to circumvent sanctions for Russia.’

He also said: ‘There is no clear evidence that China provides weaponry to Russia, but there is no doubt that China provides dual-use materials to Russia.’

Asked which side would break first in the conflict, he said that he believed Russia would ‘back down’ eventually if various developments took place, including Ukraine receiving more financial support from the European Union. He said Ukraine was facing a ‘huge budgetary gap’ of around €70 billion for the next year, with around €40 billion of this needed for ammunition.  

Asked about whether Ukraine could recover territory from Russian forces, Yatsenyuk said: ‘I want to be very realistic. Whether we can regain territory right now: Not really.’ 

But he said if the Ukrainian state is preserved, the war ends and various other conditions are met, including Ukraine getting ‘something similar to the Marshall Plan’, then ‘the time will come when Ukraine will regain its complete territorial independency.’

He said he disagreed with the framing of the war as ‘Putin’s war against Ukraine’: ‘This is the war of the Russian people who support Putin against an independent and sovereign nation, which is Ukraine.’

‘If Putin dies, another successor from KGB will take over the throne. That’s my calculus. And it means that we have to be strong enough to survive, strong enough to defend, strong enough to preserve our country,’ he said.

Yatsenyuk, who was Ukraine’s prime minister from 2014 to 2016, is the founder of the Open Ukraine Foundation and chairman of the Kyiv Security Forum.

item.title: Ukraine is running out of time
item.description:
After over four-and-a-half years of entrenched warfare, reports of U.S.-backed peace talks to end Russia's war on Ukraine are back in the news. After Finland and Norway held Europe’s first direct talks with President Vladimir Putin in a year, more trilateral talks between the U.S., Ukraine and Russia are planned for later this month.

While we’ve heard tales of imminent peace time and again, here's hoping American emissaries and their counterparts can finally bring an end to the fighting.That’s because, despite considerable efforts by the U.S. and Europe to help Ukraine win this war, there is no victory in sight. While Ukrainians arguably thwarted Russian advances in its very first weeks, its backers have failed to help Ukraine consolidate its battlefield victories at the negotiating table.

As a result, Russia’s invasion has slowly wrecked Ukraine: the war is Europe's deadliest conflict since World War II and Russia has seized approximately a fifth of Ukraine’s territory. After years of needless death and destruction, what will it take to actually forge an agreement to finally end this war?

For the latest episode of Always at War, we spoke to Anatol Lieven, journalist, author, professor, and now Director of the Eurasia Program at the Quincy Institute to discuss his career, how he became an expert on the region, and what he thinks peace can look like there.

Lieven’s diagnosis of Ukraine’s current situation is grim. He estimates that the war has killed some 200,000-250,000 Ukrainians, that millions have fled the country and are unlikely to return, and explains that the birthrate has completely collapsed. As he puts it, “the population may be half what it was in 1990.”

But what’s most shocking about the dire circumstances facing Kyiv is that they were foreseeable, and perhaps even preventable. Lieven himself predicted many of the current crises over decades of analysis, from books including Russia and Ukraine: A Fraternal Rivalry in 1999, to Quincy Institute papers on the dangers of protracted war in 2022.

What was true then is still true today: a compromise peace that secures Kyiv’s sovereignty and empowers Ukrainians to rebuild and return is a victory for Ukraine.

As Lieven has long insisted, pretending this would be anything but a victory is foolhardy: most wars “have ended not with the complete victory of one side, but with some form of messy compromise.”

Yet instead of coming to grips with the realities facing Ukraine, popular headlines continue to push narratives promising imminent victory. One possible explanation for the media’s incessant optimism is that Ukraine’s victory, understandably, feels like a moral imperative in response to Russia’s unjust war. As a result, journalists and world leaders alike are willing to indulge fantasy rather than acknowledge the gruesome truth on the ground. But Ukrainians themselves don’t have the luxury of retreating to fantasy; by a 2:1 margin, they would rather see their government prioritize ending the war as soon as possible instead of pursuing total victory.

The continued refusal by many in Washington to recognize Ukrainians’ appetites for peace, and the realities on the ground informing them, constitute a noble lie to oneself, one’s readers, or one’s constituents. It’s a lie that’s gone too far.

item.title: I know the dangers a wounded Trump presents – this is how the UK should deal with him now | Kim Darroch
item.description:

  • Kim Darroch was Britain’s ambassador to the US between January 2016 and December 2019

Election nights are party time in Washington. The bars and restaurants fill up and the city rocks. For diplomats, it’s an opportunity – but it’s also a long night, as you trek across the party scene in search of insight and illumination. Invariably, it has its moments. I recall being at the Washington Post party on the night of the presidential election on 8 November 2016. Washington is an overwhelmingly Democrat city and the atmosphere was raucously optimistic, reflecting Hillary Clinton’s small but consistent lead in the polls. As the first results came in a shocked hush fell across the room. People gathered in small, murmuring groups. Within 30 minutes, half the guests had left.

In contrast, I recall speaking to Nancy Pelosi, the queen of the Democrats, at a watch party on 6 November 2018, for the midterms during Trump’s first presidency. I asked her what I should put in my overnight report to London, given that most results wouldn’t be in. She said, with striking confidence, that I should predict that the Democrats would retake the House of Representatives. She was right: the Democrats flipped 41 Republican seats. It gave Pelosi a second term as speaker of the House and gave the world the enjoyable theatre of her sitting directly behind Trump at his State of the Union speeches, rolling her eyes at the bombast.

Kim Darroch was British ambassador to the US from 2016 to 2019, and is author of Collateral Damage: Britain, America and Europe in the Age of Trump

The Democrats have gained new powers to constrain Donald Trump. But the drubbing that Republicans received could yet prompt him to new excesses

Donald Trump is a president without parallel, but history can still be instructive. Lame duck presidents often focus on foreign policy to escape domestic discontent and establish a legacy in an area where a hostile Congress offers less of an obstacle. Mr Trump, who was stunningly rebuffed by voters in Tuesday’s midterms, might seek satisfaction in construction projects, the 2028 presidential race and his family’s future. Or, amid the humiliation and with Republican critics growing louder, he could distract attention with fresh adventurism – perhaps escalating against Cuba – or more likely a vengeful new offensive against Iran.

Mr Trump won’t put in the legwork or attention to detail demanded by, say, Bill Clinton’s push for lasting peace in the Middle East. But he loves the glitz of state visits, spectacular military action, hobnobbing with strongmen and (unearned) credit for dubious “peace deals”. item.title: The hypersonic missile race is an unnecessary boondoggle for US
item.description:
Last year, a group of high-ranking former military personnel and weapons company executives issued an ominous warning in an Atlantic Council report. U.S. adversaries, they said, were making rapid advances in hypersonic missile technology, “posing a severe challenge to US battlefield dominance.”

“Now is the time to act decisively to close the hypersonic gap and defend the nation’s interests for the future,” the report declared.

But is this really an existential threat? Will these technologies be as truly groundbreaking as the defense-tech industry claims? Experts who spoke with RS cast doubt on these positions, arguing that the spending is wasteful because despite the hype, hypersonics won’t provide unique advantages for the United States.

Hypersonic missiles can reach speeds of over Mach 5 and remain maneuverable mid-flight to confuse defensive systems. The missiles are designed to evade traditional ballistic missile defense systems by flying at low altitude, leaving them difficult to detect until minutes or even seconds before striking a target. In comparison, traditional ballistics follow high, extraatmospheric, parabolic arcs, allowing radar systems to detect them before they reach their zenith, sometimes affording defenders more than 20 minutes of warning before impact.

Claims about the difficulty of intercepting hypersonics aren’t airtight. Despite successful tests of some hypersonics, some experts doubt the feasibility of the claimed maximum speeds, maneuverability, and stealth abilities, according to Scientific American. The Congressional Budget Office agrees, insisting that “technological challenges must still be overcome to field hypersonic missiles.” According to the CBO, if fielded, the weapons would cost at least 30% more per unit than their ballistic counterparts. Even then, they would be more useful than ballistics only against extremely advanced, long-range defense systems, which no US adversaries currently possess.

Still, claims of successful tests or deployments of hypersonics by Russia, China, North Korea, and Iran have caused concern in the national security establishment about growing risks to Washington’s aerial dominance and, particularly, the ability of these weapons to get past U.S. missile defense systems. As of October 2026, Russia has reportedly tested two maneuvering hypersonic systems, and it has used regular hypersonic missiles (Oreshnik) in the war against Ukraine.

Iran and North Korea’s claims of hypersonic capabilities remain unverified by independent observers. China has a confirmed hypersonic weapon, with unconfirmed reports suggesting additional successes.

The chase for hypersonics ignores a larger geopolitical context, says Kelly Greico of the Stimson Center , who argues the United States’ major adversaries are acting out of a sense of vulnerability rather than a desire for escalation. For Russia and China, this stems from the transfer of U.S. THAAD (Terminal High Altitude Area Defense) missile defense systems into Ukraine and South Korea. U.S. adversaries see these batteries as giving cover to U.S. activities in their respective regions, making it easier for the U.S. to attack without having to worry too much about defending its equipment and personnel in the region. If hypersonics can evade such defenses, these countries can theoretically respond effectively to any American incursions in the region, thus acting as a deterrent.

In this context, these advanced, but expensive and rare, munitions make strategic sense. For a country like Iran, which can manufacture missiles more cheaply and has more limited resources, investing in a few highly advanced long-range missiles to increase deterrence in a future conflict makes strategic sense. In hypothetical wars — and indeed, in the ongoing war in the Persian Gulf — Iran is defending itself close to home against a militarily superior enemy. A country like Iran or China knows that even the threat of a strike to key U.S. sites, or even against the American homeland, would be intolerable for the U.S. and perhaps prevent an attack.

However, Greico felt that, given expensive military supply chains, a less developed missile manufacturing sector, and a different overall strategic orientation, these munitions would do little to enhance American security. The U.S. typically aims to maintain aerial superiority to carry out offensive strikes against an enemy with comparably minimal aerial defenses. Greico says existing, cheaper ballistic missiles launched en masse would be just as effective at evading or overwhelming any countermeasures. Additionally, she believes the United States’ nuclear triad already serves as a more than effective nuclear deterrent that wouldn’t be improved by hypersonic development.

Yet the U.S. is moving ahead with large-scale hypersonics development. Recently, the Pentagon offered private industry incentives to help close the alleged gap, with procurement contracts totaling over $12 billion for FY 2027. This staggering sum excludes additional research and development spending. Although traditional players like Boeing, Lockheed Martin, and Northrop Grumman are in the mix, defense-tech startups are also trying their hand. Pentagon procurement overhauls in 2025 changed the rules to benefit younger, more innovative companies. Since then, venture capital investment in the hypersonic sector has more than tripled, rising to $1.2 billion in 2025 from $220 million the year prior.

Newcomer Castelion demonstrates this trend well. As of September 2026, the company is valued at $14 billion after raising $1 billion in Series C funding, largely from venture capital, and winning nearly $500 million in Defense Department contracts this year alone. In September 2026, the Navy placed a nearly $44 million order for 444 rounds of the Castellion hypersonic strike missile, known as the Blackbeard, making it one of its largest such contracts to date.

Greico advised caution toward large-scale investment in immature technologies like hypersonics.

Pointing to a Government Accountability Office (GAO) report, Greico said the projects are already behind schedule. The GAO reported in July that the Army and Navy alone have already approved over $50 billion in investments and procurement of hypersonic missile technologies. As of July, the Navy Conventional Prompt Strike (CPS) Program is 24 months behind on modifying ships to carry the $50 million-a-piece CPS missiles. The Dark Eagle, a missile developed jointly by the Army and Navy that will serve as the backbone of the Army’s hypersonic arsenal, is already delayed by two years.

There is no central strategy for hypersonic investment. Julia Gledhill, a researcher and defense budgetary expert at the Stimson Center, explained there is no easy way to get a single number for the total U.S. investment in hypersonics today. “You have hypersonic funding in Golden Dome, in the Defense Production Act Money that is focused on industrial base expansion,” she said, adding that they were on the new Pentagon Munitions Acceleration Council’s list of 12 critical munitions.

Greico and Gledhill both said any strategic gains from hypersonics would be marginal at best and that greater investment risked entering a costly escalatory spending cycle with countries like Russia and China, as each strives to gain a technological upper hand with increasingly complex counter systems. Gledhill pointed to Trump’s “Golden Dome for America” as an example, comparing it to the ill-fated Reagan-era “Star Wars” initiative. Estimated to cost at least $1.2 trillion over 20 years, the program aims to build an orbital nuclear missile defense system. Scientists have already dubbed it a “fantasy,” and experts say it would be an unprecedented escalation in militarizing space.

Greico offered a simple explanation for why Washington is continuing this pursuit despite its myriad challenges. Hypersonic investment is “a culture thing,” she said. “There seems to be discomfort with being behind.”

One Parts Bin, Three Wars: Beijing built a valve. We built a wall.
item.description:
Welcome to The Iron Triangle, the Cipher Brief column serving Procurement Officers tasked with buying the future, Investors funding the next generation of defense technology, and the Policy Wonks analyzing its impact on the global order.

In the industrial parks of Guangdong, the hardest part of the drone war is the visitor schedule. Ukrainian drone makers who travel to their Chinese component suppliers describe hosts who choreograph visits so that Ukrainian and Russian buyers never share a building. Separate doors. Service corridors. Empty conference rooms. Oleksandr Yakovenko, founder of TAF Industries, one of Ukraine's largest drone producers, told the Financial Times that his suppliers "try to make it so we will not be in the same factory at the same time." By the paper's account, the car carrying the Russians pulls out and the car carrying the Ukrainians pulls in.

That is not a supplier. That is a referee. And this month the referee is rewriting the rules.

The Valve

On October 19, Beijing published Announcement No. 49, revising dual-use export controls on 13 categories of drone components and technology, effective November 18. It reaches heavy multirotor motors and speed controllers, long-range autopilots, inertial navigation, datalinks, and engines. Read the signature block before the parts list: the notice was issued by the Ministry of Commerce, the General Administration of Customs, and the Equipment Development Department of the Central Military Commission. The military's equipment office co-signed Beijing's drone controls in 2023 too. This was never trade policy.

The design matters more than the scope. Announcement 49 bans nothing. It requires licenses, and licensing allows treatment to differ by exporter, destination, and end user. A ban is a wall. A license is a valve, and Beijing keeps its hand on it.

The second date resolved itself the day this column went to the editor, and the way it resolved is the point. China's suspension of its sweeping October 2025 rare earth controls, the ones that reach any foreign product containing as little as 0.1 percent Chinese-origin rare earth by value, was due to lapse on November 10. For six weeks the diplomacy said January while the legal notice said November. On November 9, with one day to spare, Beijing extended the pause to January 10. Two months. Nothing closed, and every magnet buyer in the West spent the autumn planning for a license queue anyway. A valve does not have to turn to work. It only has to be seen in someone's hand.

Three Wars, One Parts Bin

Start with what these parts do. By the Financial Times's count, drones account for up to three quarters of recent losses in Ukraine. The parts bin is where the killing power comes from.

Moscow. China's share of Russia's imports of the goods the G7 flags as battlefield priorities rose from 54.3 percent in 2022 to 84.6 percent in 2025. Russia does not have a supply chain. It has a supplier.

Kyiv. Ukraine has worked to get out. At the start of 2024, nearly 90 percent of its imported drone components came directly from China. In the first eight months of 2026, the figure was 28 percent. The number flatters. Some of the parts arriving through Poland and the Czech Republic were most likely made in China too, and Yakovenko told the Associated Press that switching entirely to Western parts could raise costs by as much as 60 percent and cut production by about the same. Andrii Taganskyi, whose company Odd Systems builds drone cameras, summed up the rest: "Without this 5%, there is no camera."

Then there is the detail that should keep Brussels up at night. In July, the EU let Kyiv spend part of a €5.9 billion drone tranche of its defense loan on Chinese components, because Europe cannot make enough of them. That loan is money Europe borrowed on the capital markets, to be repaid if Russia ever pays reparations. So European debt, backed by a Russian IOU, buys Chinese parts for Ukrainian drones, from the same supplier base arming Russia. Nobody planned that, but everybody signed it.

Taipei, by way of Washington. If you think the valve only turns for Europe's war, ask Skydio. In October 2024, Beijing sanctioned America's largest drone maker after Washington approved defense assistance for Taiwan. Chinese authorities visited Skydio's suppliers, including a TDK battery subsidiary in Dongguan, and told them to stop. Skydio rationed batteries to one per drone. Its only customer in Taiwan, the company pointed out, was the National Fire Agency. Its customer in Ukraine had ordered thousands of drones. A decision about Taiwan became battery rationing at the company supplying Ukraine. One parts bin, three wars.

The Wall We Built

Washington's answer has been prohibitions. On January 1, the DFARS magnet restriction expands to bar contractors from delivering neodymium-iron-boron and samarium-cobalt magnets if any step in the chain, from mining through refining, melting, and finished production, takes place in a covered country. Since September 3, Proclamation 11055 has imposed Section 232 duties of 10 to 100 percent on imported drones and components.

Each measure is defensible. Together they make a wall with very little stacked behind it. On June 30, the Army opened its first domestic small-drone motor line at Tobyhanna Army Depot, 1,500 motors a day. Adamas Intelligence, which tracks the magnet trade, reports that the magnets inside those motors are still roughly 90 percent Chinese-made. The Pentagon knows it. In May, the Defense Logistics Agency placed $25.8 million in sole-source orders with two U.S.-based magnet makers and paid $2 million to qualify a third. Set $25.8 million beside a program buying drones by the hundred thousand. The magnet rule has exceptions, including one for commercial off-the-shelf items, and they will be used, because the alternative is an idle motor line. A wall you have to keep waiving is not a wall. This is not a scandal. It is a feature of buying the airframe and hoping the bill of materials sorts itself out.

The tariff has its own irony. Taiwan, the democracy building a "non-red" drone supply chain as national policy, is slated to pay a reduced but real 15 percent combined rate on its drones. We are taxing the exit.

For the Procurement Officer

The Drone Dominance Program wants more than 200,000 one-way attack drones. Call it 800,000 motors. Chinese brushless motors have sold for $12 to $25 against $100 to $225 for American equivalents. Those were smaller motors at last year's prices, so treat the result as an order of magnitude: the premium to buy every one of those motors outside China lands somewhere around $60 to $170 million. The program is worth $1.1 billion. Independence for the most exposed component costs less than a rounding error on Golden Dome. You are not short of money. You are short of a contract that buys components instead of airframes.

The Investment Thesis

The bottleneck premium is moving down the bill of materials. Airframe makers are plentiful; hundreds applied to fly the Gauntlet. Magnet makers, motor winders, and camera-sensor houses that can document a clean chain back to the mine are not. On January 1, the documentation becomes the product. Price accordingly.

The Policy Wonk's Warning

Beijing has built the only arms-control regime of the drone age that is actually effective. No treaty, no verification, no Senate ratification. Just a licensing desk that can decide, case by case, whose drones fly in Ukraine. It has already used that desk to punish a Taiwan decision. Assume it will do so again when the Strait gets tense, and that the first sign will be paperwork, not ships.

My Take.

We do not need a wall. We need our own valve, and building one takes three moves.

First, pool demand. Washington's Drone Dominance money and Europe's Ukraine loan should buy components, not just finished drones, on multi-year offtake contracts that a magnet plant can take to a bank.

Second, write one list. Taiwan's ITRI is already the only overseas certifier in the U.S.-led Green UAS program. On October 27, at a forum in Taipei co-hosted by Taiwan's foreign ministry, John Hemmings of the Henry Jackson Society proposed that Taiwan and Europe agree on a red-free standard, certify suppliers, and stand up a drone supply chain office to write the testing rules. Fold Ukraine in, add the United States, and make it one certified-supplier list across the alliance.

Third, make the list worth something. Certified allied components should enter at zero duty. The proclamation already carves out zero-rate lanes for approved onshoring plans. Extend that logic to allies who are onshoring for all of us.

That is how a parts bin becomes an alliance.

The Risk.

The valve leaks. Ukrainian firms keep finding ways around Chinese restrictions through intermediaries, and Chinese factories have little appetite for losing a customer that size. Announcement 49 also aims high: standard five- and seven-inch FPVs fall below its motor thresholds, while heavy-lift and long-range systems take the hit. A fair reader could say Beijing is managing a market, not picking a winner. My answer is the last six weeks. Beijing closed nothing, and the West planned around it anyway. A regime that can be precise is more dangerous than one that is blunt, because it can squeeze one end user without disturbing anyone else's quarterly numbers.

Conclusion

Somewhere in Shenzhen this week, a sales manager is timing the cars in the parking lot so that two warring delegations never meet. America has already had its visit. In 2024 the men who came to the factory were Chinese officials, and the customer they cut off was ours. If Beijing can already decide which side's drones fly over Ukraine, what makes us so confident it will not decide whose fly over the Strait?

item.title: Iran Is Poking The Bear
item.description:
Tehran has been playing a dangerous game of chicken with the U.S. administration for months. With the just concluded midterms now in hand, they risk making a dangerous miscalculation just when it matters most. This is unlikely to end well.

With the continuation of strikes this week against international shipping transiting the Strait of Hormuz, while simultaneously engaging in renewed negotiations, Tehran is poking the bear with one hand while feeding it with the other. This is a dangerous strategy; they could lose a hand… or worse.

The Iranian leadership is clearly trying to have it both ways. Equal parts emboldened and wary, with a hefty dose of economic reality rapidly bearing down upon them.

Tehran is and always has been a keen observer of American politics. This time, however, they appear to be overconfident, and potentially risk acting on a tragic misreading of the situation. This two-pronged strategy - continued taunting, both verbal and military, while offering to negotiate, sort of – appears to indicate they perceive a deep new vulnerability in their opponent given the historic drubbing the administration received in the midterms. That is possible, and the administration will certainly face harsh scrutiny over its handling of the war. But it is also possible that they are seeing a President Trump who is merely stunned and, if such a thing is possible… humbled, if only for the moment. But this humility is unlikely to last. The President retains primary control over U.S. foreign and military policy, and there are already reports of plans for massive new strikes if negotiations again fail, or the President becomes frustrated with Tehran’s usual stalling and stubbornness.

The President is already looking for a fall-guy within his administration for a failed, unpopular war, and the devastating impact on the midterms; with the odds-on favorite(s) being Secretary of Defense Hegseth and/or senior military leaders. He is almost certain to look for one outside his administration as well, with Iran the certain candidate for their unwillingness to accede to the President’s attempts at diplomacy pre-election. He has proven that he is nothing if not vengeful. At the same time, the President wants a deal and appears ready for one. Unless, that is, Tehran insists on rubbing his face in a less than optimal resolution. This risks a reaction that would serve no one.

Tehran’s hubris is legend. As is that of President Trump. When these meet head-to-head – hubris to hubris – the result is at best uncertain, and potentially disastrous.

In the end, the most likely conclusion remains a negotiated settlement. Iran has several advantages, including geography, proven resilience and staying power. And their just-concluded conclave with Russia is a new, ominous development that bodes ill. On the other hand, the U.S. administration may finally have an effective strategy in its naval/economic blockade. But this will take time, and it may no longer have the political runway to see it through.

Tehran should declare victory and allow the U.S. President to go home. Face-saving measures are essential for both sides to avoid the additional death and destruction that is sure to follow military escalation, by either side.

But this will not be the final bell. Tehran will be left to its own devices to face the enormous challenges of a shattered economy, a degraded environment, and a restive population.

This is not over by a long shot.

I am reposting portions of a previous post given their continued relevance

Iran Is “Counting Coup” On The United States!

“Iran is playing a very dangerous game. In the face of the awesome military power of the United States, in between desultory negotiating sessions, they continue to touch the enemy by launching attacks against U.S. and allied Gulf facilities. Recently, they have reached farther afield, striking U.S. assets in an Egyptian port. This would seem to be inexplicable behavior, given the U.S.’s obvious desire for a deal, inviting as it has strong retaliatory strikes against Iran’s increasingly beleaguered military, and potentially civilian, infrastructure. Most recently, we are seeing reports of possible Iranian cyberattacks on the water supplies of U.S. cities; such activities are certain to continue and likely to escalate, plausibly deniable and effective in sowing fear as they are. The question is why?”

“It may be simple hubris. It may be a misread of the desperation of their opponent. Or simply overconfidence in the strength of their position. It most certainly is part and parcel of a purposeful negotiating strategy, a reminder to all involved that Iranian forces can reach out and touch you whenever they wish.

Regardless, they are walking a fine line, and they have placed this conflict squarely in the crosshairs of unintended consequences.

As they so often do, they risk overreaching. Should one of these missile or drone strikes make it through, whether by luck or skill, and inflict truly significant casualties on U.S. personnel, either in a land-based facility or on a naval vessel for example, this could surge American support for a massive response, possibly including – however unlikely – ground troops, radically altering and escalating the course of this conflict.”

“The Iranian leadership’s actions, however, are likely aimed not only at the United States but may be the result of continued factional maneuvering in Tehran, as groups jockey for advantage for what comes next. Now that it appears likely the regime will survive, they are no doubt looking ahead to where they will land in a new regime. As both factions and individuals.”

As I wrote in ‘Is Iran Controlling the Gulf Conflict?’: “I would posit that the newly ascended Supreme Leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, may in fact be a phantom leader. Alive in some fashion, perhaps largely incapacitated, but not actually in charge. And even if able to coherently express his views, in no way nearly as powerful or influential as his father. The seemingly reckless actions of the regime in courting U.S. retaliation may in actuality reflect a lack of a coherent decision-making process as opposed to a unified one. I think it is quite possible that competing factions within the regime are using Mojtaba as an avatar while they maneuver for decisive advantage.”

On 15 May, I laid out in “Ground Hog Day”, a recommended way forward for the U.S. that I think largely still applies. It is a measure of how fruitless continued military action is that these remain relevant today:

“Make a deal with Iran. One that they will accept. This will require painful concessions and is certain to include provisions that many will find objectionable, including significant sanctions relief. And it will leave the Iranian regime in place and in control of Iran. For now.”

“As much as I would prefer to see regime change in Iran, I believe a deal may be the only realistic way out of the Groundhog Day-like doom loop in which we find ourselves. Simply put, the administration squandered the initial opportunity presented by a unique confluence of events by its lack of strategic planning and a fundamental misunderstanding of Iran and the Iranian regime.”

“As a result, we are going to have to step back and take a longer view. I pity the people of Iran, at least in the near term. They are certain to suffer the brunt of the regime’s immediate ire. That is a hard truth.”

“This is not, however, the end of the story. Iran’s internal weaknesses still matter–and may shape what comes next more than battlefield successes. I am cautiously, very cautiously optimistic that even barring regime change, Iran’s leadership will be forced to change direction.”

“The issues facing Iran prior to the War were serious, in fact existential – a collapsing economy, hyper-inflation, severe water shortages, lack of electricity, and growing widespread popular anger and unrest – and are ongoing and only getting worse. Whatever the Iranian leadership looks like, it will have to address these issues. And it is not clear that they will be capable of doing this without outside help. This is where the U.S. and hopefully our Western allies come in: sanctions relief, and extensive economic and other assistance in exchange for real changes in policy and a pullback on objectionable activities and programs. The potential for this may, and I say may, have increased with the removal of Ali Khamenei from the Supreme Leader’s seat. But it will depend on whether his son and successor, Mojtaba, is less rigidly ideological than his father. We will see if he is willing to put the Iranian people ahead of the regime.”

It is becoming more obvious by the day that the U.S. needs to come to a negotiated settlement with Iran. And the terms of this settlement are certain to be painful and unsatisfactory from the perspective of the West. But continuing tit-for-tat airstrikes simply prolongs the pain and risks horrific unintended consequences without solving the problem, as well as providing the regime with a distraction from its appalling management of Iran’s economy, natural resources, and foreign policy.

An enraged and restive Iranian population awaits. Let the regime face, without fear or favor, the fruits of its mismanagement, leaving it to confront what it fears most: the streets. This is likely where genuine regime change will occur.

Nov 13 (Reuters) - The US military denied Iran's claim on Friday to have attacked a US early-warning radar in Bahrain, saying its forces had shot down two one-way attack drones launched by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps toward Bahrain with no harm caused.

Iran had said its strike was in retaliation for what it described as an air attack on a telecommunications tower in its Hormozgan province, according to Iranian state media.

item.title: Turkey, Qatar sign mutual defence agreement
item.description:
Turkey and Qatar announced on Friday that they signed a mutual defence agreement, which they said was aimed at adopting a "unified position" in the face of an external attack.

The announcement came after Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan met Qatari Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani in Istanbul.

Erdogan had said the agreement would further strengthen ties between the regional allies, according to his office.

Qatar's ruler travelled to Istanbul after attending the United Nations COP31 climate summit in southern Turkey.

item.title: UN rights chief demands Houthis return body of Yemeni staff member
item.description:
GENEVA, Nov 13 (Reuters) - The UN's human rights chief on Friday demanded the return of the body of a Yemeni staff member of his office who died of unknown causes weeks ago after being held in Houthi custody for more than two years.

Mohammad el Shami's family learned of his death on October 30, more than a month after it occurred, but they have received no explanation of the cause or circumstances. El Shami had been held by the Houthi group since June ​6, 2024.

item.title: Turkey, Qatar sign mutual defence agreement, pledge unified stance against attack
item.description:
ISTANBUL, Nov 13 (Reuters) - Turkey and Qatar signed a mutual defence agreement on Friday aimed at strengthening collective defence and promoting regional security, and pledged a unified stance against any external armed attack targeting either country, according to a joint statement issued after talks between their leaders.

The two sides agreed to consult on threats to their security, as well as regional and global security issues and defence policies, and to expand cooperation through joint military exercises, defence-industry cooperation and personnel training exchanges.
